source.title: The Quantization Model of Neural Scaling
source.authors: Eric J. Michaud; Zi-Ming Liu; Uzay Girit; Max Tegmark

record.file_problem: The full paper is present, though unrelated garbled text snippets are interspersed in the extracted text.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures loss scaling on Pythia models and a synthetic task using its own quantization-model analysis, rather than reproducing the original scaling-law methods.
record.gate_note: The paper reports Pythia parameter and training-step loss scaling and synthetic-task scaling in parameters, steps, and data. It does not test compute-optimal allocation or downstream-task predictability. Prior studies' results cited in the paper are not recorded as rows; the QDG cluster-frequency analysis is not itself a measurement of loss scaling.
record.test_reason: The paper's own Pythia evaluations measure held-out loss against non-embedding parameters (fit αN≈0.083 over the first six models, with the 6.4b model breaking the trend) and against training steps. Its synthetic multitask sparse-parity experiments measure power-law loss scaling in parameters, steps and multi-epoch data. The method is a different, theory-driven approach (quantization model) rather than a replication of Kaplan or Chinchilla fitting.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors argue that discrete skills ('quanta') learned in order of power-law use frequency can explain power-law scaling and emergence, and they demonstrate this on a synthetic task. On Pythia they report a parameter power law (αN≈0.083) for the first six models, noting that 6.4b breaks the trend. They tentatively find QDG cluster sizes roughly compatible with the theory, while stressing that this measurement is highly uncertain.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes a quantization-based explanation, evaluates Pythia losses and a synthetic multitask sparse-parity task, and does not reproduce the original studies' scaling-law fitting or compute-optimal allocation procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: On the synthetic task, scaling-exponent relationships vary with the task distribution parameter α; data-scaling results are affected by early stopping, and training-step scaling differs from the theoretical prediction.

fits_no_version.finding: On the synthetic task, step and data scaling exponents differ from the quantization theory's predictions: αS≈0.45 versus 0.29 predicted, and subtask convergence scales as p^-0.81 rather than p^-1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Quantization-model predictions of scaling exponents from task-frequency exponents hold only approximately.

record.problems: The 6.4b Pythia point does not fit the parameter curve and is excluded from the exponent estimate. The parameter-scaling exponent is estimated from the first six points without an uncertainty interval stated. The paper notes that parameter-scaling results on the toy task are noisy and may depend on initialization; the data-scaling experiments use the same seed and model size across runs. The authors also describe the QDG-derived frequency estimate as highly uncertain.
record.rows_left_out: No reported loss-scaling results were left out.

untested.parts: Compute scaling is not tested. Token scaling is shown only through within-run training curves, not separate runs trained to completion.
There is no prospective extrapolation across orders of magnitude. The only out-of-fit point is a single model less than one order of magnitude larger.
Image, video, fine-tuning and transfer settings are not tested. Only a synthetic sparse-parity MLP task is studied, including multi-epoch (repeated) data.
Not tested. Emergence is discussed only per-token or per-subtask, not on downstream tasks.
Parameter counting, fitting methods and compute-optimal split are not compared. Language-model evidence on V7 is limited to the 6.4b break.

missing.what: Individual Pythia model sizes and their mean test losses behind the αN fit; the size and direction of the 6.4b deviation
Step-exponent (αS) and data-exponent (αD) values across the full range of α settings

record.verdict_notes: Appendix F's compilation of exponents from prior studies is cited data, not the study's own results, and is correctly left out of the rows. Neither original source is this paper, so verdicts are allowed. The V5 support rests on a dataset engineered to have Zipfian subtask frequencies, so it shows the power-law form can arise in a new setting rather than that it arises naturally.

versions.untested_parts: The language-model evidence is parameter scaling; the paper does not test loss scaling in training tokens or compute with other factors held non-bottlenecked.
The study does not report a prospective prediction protocol or establish an extrapolation across a stated number of orders of magnitude.
The synthetic multitask sparse-parity task is a different training setting, but the study does not test image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The study does not test compute-optimal allocation, alternative parameter-counting methods, or a controlled comparison of fitting methods.

rows.measure: Relationship between empirical parameter exponent αN and task-distribution α
rows.value: The relationship deviates from the prediction: αN is below α for small α and above α for large α.
rows.note: The paper says the scaling curves appear to remain power laws, while the relationship between exponents varies with α.
rows.check: Relabelled. The baseline is the paper's own theory (αN=α), not a published scaling law. What bears on V7 is that the fitted exponent changes with the data distribution α while curves stay power laws, so the state for V7 is observed, not partial. This is a synthetic setting.

rows.operation_detail: Compared training-step scaling exponents and subtask convergence time with theoretical predictions
rows.measure: Mean test loss versus steps; convergence steps versus subtask frequency
rows.baseline: Theory predicts αS ≈ 0.29 and convergence steps proportional to p_k^-1
rows.value: Empirical αS ≈ 0.45; convergence time follows approximately p_k^-0.81 rather than p_k^-1.
rows.note: The authors say convergence is faster than expected for many subtasks, producing a steeper scaling curve.
rows.check: This compares the step exponent with the paper's own theoretical prediction at a single α. It shows no dependence on setup or fitting choices, so it does not bear on V7 as stated.

conditions.value: Early stopping used for loss curves

rows.measure: Mean test loss versus training samples; number of learned subtasks n versus training samples
rows.baseline: Theory predicts αD = α/(α + 1) and n proportional to D^(1/(α+1))
rows.value: αD is substantially above the prediction for small α; the authors report that n is approximately proportional to D^(1/(α+1)) when including subtasks learned after early stopping.
rows.note: The authors suggest early stopping may cut off training before all subtasks are learned.
rows.check: For V7, the relevant point is that the data exponent depends on the data distribution and on the training procedure. Early stopping cuts off learning and inflates αD relative to theory. The baseline is the authors' theory, not a published law.
